title: PHP Statements, Expressions, and Blocks
learning_outcomes: Explain what php statements, expressions, and blocks contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: statements and expressions.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: PHP source is parsed and executed by the PHP runtime. Tags mark PHP regions, statements and blocks define the program structure, and CLI and web-server execution have different inputs and output contexts. In this lesson, focus on statements and expressions; then compare it with semicolons. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use php statements, expressions, and blocks when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: PHP source is parsed and executed by the PHP runtime. Tags mark PHP regions, statements and blocks define the program structure, and CLI and web-server execution have different inputs and output contexts. For php statements, expressions, and blocks, begin with statements and expressions. Also distinguish semicolons; braces and statement blocks; whitespace and formatting. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Use the smallest representative example, make expected behavior explicit, and test normal plus boundary inputs.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for php statements, expressions, and blocks from top to bottom. Start by identifying statements and expressions, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

content.task: Create a second small example for php statements, expressions, and blocks that demonstrates "statements and expressions". Before running it, write down the expected result and one boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example includes a clear use of statements and expressions.
The learner can explain its input, rule, and observable output.
At least one edge case is tested or documented.
hints: Start with the most direct listed subtopic and a single input.
Keep the example small enough that you can predict the output manually.
Test one normal case and one empty, invalid, or boundary case.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
